candidates.title: Stop Playing GTA 6 Game! SHOCKING $1 Billion 'Productivity Loss' Explained! #shorts
candidates.description: GTA 6’s Record Launch Revives Debate Over Lost Work Hours and Massive Earnings The release of Grand Theft Auto VI has sparked two very different economic conversations: how much money the game can make, and how many people may have taken time off to play it. GTA 6 launched on November 19, 2026. Its publisher, Take-Two Interactive, estimates that worldwide retail sales reached $3.79 billion on the first day alone. That is a remarkable start, but retail sales are not the same as company profit: development, marketing, distribution and other costs still have to be accounted for. The comparison with GTA 5 shows why expectations are so high. Take-Two reported that the earlier game passed $1 billion in worldwide retail sales during its first three days in 2013. It has since sold nearly 235 million units, while GTA Online has kept the franchise commercially active for years. That history points to GTA 6’s long-term earning potential beyond launch-week purchases. Meanwhile, viral posts claim the launch could cause $1 billion in lost productivity as gamers skip work. That figure has no verified study behind it. One US workplace-data study did find that requests for November 19 leave were running 13% above comparable dates, but it does not prove the game caused every request or establish a dollar loss. There is no reliable equivalent estimate for India. For Indian gamers, GTA 6 is already a major entertainment launch. Its first-day sales are measurable; the claims about a productivity crisis remain speculation. candidates.title: This Japanese pronunciation trick trips up almost every beginner 🤏
candidates.description: Here's a Japanese pronunciation trick that trips up almost every beginner 🤏 The small っ (called sokuon) isn't pronounced like a letter, it's a short pause that doubles the next consonant sound. And it completely changes the word. おと (oto) means "sound," but おっと (otto) means "husband." きて (kite) means "come," but きって (kitte) means "stamp." さか (saka) is a slope, and さっか (sakka) is a writer. Getting this beat right is a big step toward sounding natural when you speak Japanese, and it's why reading hiragana carefully matters from day one. candidates.title: Why Closing This Narrow Waterway Panics the Entire World
candidates.description: Look at this narrow 21-mile gap of water between Iran and Oman—when conflict threatens to shut it down, global energy markets panic overnight. Why can't oil tankers just take a detour around it? Known as the Strait of Hormuz, this critical maritime chokepoint is the only sea exit out of the Persian Gulf. Unlike the Suez Canal or Red Sea, there is no alternate ocean route—meaning any blockade instantly traps roughly 20% of the world's oil and LNG supply and sends global fuel prices skyrocketing. candidates.title: Master your reactions, or someone else may master your decisions. #machivelli #psychology #shorts
candidates.description: ♟️ THE PERSON WHO UNDERSTANDS YOUR REACTIONS MAY UNDERSTAND HOW TO INFLUENCE YOU. "A person who can predict your reaction has already learned how to influence your decisions." — Niccolò Machiavelli Human behaviour follows patterns. The words that trigger you, the situations that make you uncomfortable, and the emotions that cloud your judgment can reveal more about you than you realize. When someone understands these patterns, they may begin anticipating how you will respond. 🧠 Self-awareness is one of the strongest forms of protection against manipulation. If anger controls your responses, others may provoke you. If approval controls your decisions, others may exploit your need for acceptance. If fear dictates your choices, you may surrender opportunities without even realizing it. ⚔️ The answer isn't to become emotionless or suspicious of everyone. It's to understand your emotions without allowing them to make every decision for you. Learn to pause before reacting. Question your impulses. Recognize your patterns. Remember: The moment you understand what controls your reactions, you begin taking control of your choices. 👑 True strength isn't predicting everyone else's next move. It's refusing to let someone else's expectations dictate yours. 📖 Attribution: This quote is attributed to Niccolò Machiavelli, but its authenticity as an original quotation from his writings has not been independently verified. 🖤 SILENTTRUTH Philosophy • Psychology • Human Nature • Wisdom 🔔 Subscribe to SilentTruth and turn on the notification bell for deeper insights into philosophy, psychology, power, strategy, and human nature. #machivelli #philosophy #psychology #human nature #darkpsychology #selfawareness #emotionalintelligence #mindset #wisdom #shorts

candidates.title: The 2,000-Year-Old Vending Machine
candidates.description: About two thousand years ago, you could buy holy water from a machine. An engineer in Alexandria, Hero (Heron) of Alexandria, described it in his book Pneumatica. You drop a five-drachma coin through a slot in the top of a bronze vessel. The coin lands on a small plate at one end of a lever. The other end of the lever holds a lid that plugs a little box at the bottom of a water tank. The coin's weight tips the plate down, the lid lifts, and water runs out through a pipe. But the tilted plate lets the coin slide off, the lid drops back into place, and the water stops. Hero wrote that the lid must be heavier than the plate, but lighter than the plate and the coin together. It's a seesaw: get on, the other end goes up; get off, it comes back down. In the same book he also described a ball that spins on jets of steam, the aeolipile, more than sixteen hundred years before the first working steam engine. So today, when you drop a coin in a box and wait for it to pour you a drink, you're using one of the oldest machines in the world. #shorts #animation #history #ancientgreece #invention #vendingmachine #funfacts #didyouknow #explained

candidates.title: Why 0.999... Is Mathematically Equal to 1
candidates.description: 0.999... is not "almost 1" — it is literally another way of writing the exact number 1. This 10-second visual explainer breaks down why the repeating decimal 0.999... equals 1 using a single 1×1 unit square and four classic mathematical proofs: The Fraction Proof: 1/3 = 0.333..., so multiplying both sides by 3 gives 3/3 = 0.999... = 1. The Algebraic Proof: Setting x = 0.999... and subtracting it from 10x = 9.999... leaves 9x = 9, so x = 1. The Infinite Geometric Series: Adding 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... fills the entire unit square with zero leftover space. The Number Line: Between any two distinct real numbers, you can always fit another number. Because 1 − 0.999... = 0, no number exists between them. Key insight: Our intuition trips up because we expect every real number to have only one decimal representation. In reality, any terminating decimal (like 1 or 0.5) can also be written as an infinite repeating 9s decimal (0.999... or 0.4999...). Save this Short as a quick reference for calculus, real analysis, or the next time this math debate comes up. #Mathematics #0999Equals1 #MathExplained

candidates.title: Not every mind sees beyond the surface. #machiavelli #psychology #shorts
candidates.description: ♟️ THE DEEPEST MINDS OFTEN MAKE ONE DANGEROUS ASSUMPTION: THAT OTHERS THINK LIKE THEM. “The greatest weakness of a powerful mind is believing that everyone else thinks as deeply as it does.” — Niccolò Machiavelli One of the greatest mistakes intelligent people can make is assuming that everyone observes, analyzes, and understands the world in the same way they do. But human minds operate differently. Some people question everything. Others accept what they are told. Some recognize hidden patterns, while others see only what is immediately visible. 🧠 Intelligence is not just about understanding the world. It is also about understanding how differently other people perceive it. Never assume that everyone shares your depth of thought, your intentions, or your ability to recognize consequences. Learn to observe before judging. Listen before assuming. Understand people's actions rather than expecting everyone to think according to your own principles. 👁️ The more you understand human nature, the less you expect everyone to understand you. But remember: depth of thought should bring humility, not superiority. There is always something another mind can teach you. ♟️ Wisdom begins when you stop assuming that everyone sees the world through your eyes. 💭 Do you think most misunderstandings happen because people have different opinions, or because they think at different levels? 🖤 SILENTTRUTH Philosophy • Psychology • Human Nature • Wisdom 🔔 Subscribe to SilentTruth and turn on the notification bell for thought-provoking insights into philosophy, psychology, intelligence, and human nature. #machiavelli #philosophy #psychology #human nature #intelligence #deepthinking #wisdom #mindset #criticalthinking #shorts

candidates.title: 5 Photography Tips for Beginners
candidates.description: “Thinking about getting into photography? Yesterday I was talking with a young woman who wanted to learn, and I shared a few things I wish someone had told me when I was starting out. Here are five tips you can try this week. One. Learn what your camera settings actually do. Shutter speed freezes motion, aperture changes how much of the scene is sharp, and ISO can help when the light is low. Change one setting at a time and see what happens. Two. Look at the light before you take the picture. Photograph the same thing in direct sun, in open shade, and beside a window. You’ll see how much the light changes the mood. Three. Give yourself a place to learn. I told her to check out Kelby training for lessons on camera basics and Photoshop. Pick one lesson, then go try it with your own photos. Four. Get to know Adobe Camera Raw. Start with exposure and white balance. Take a picture that looks a little too dark or too yellow and see what two small adjustments can do. Five. Learn Levels in Photoshop. Start by adjusting the shadows, midtones, and highlights. Then try the individual red, green, and blue channels to see how Levels can help correct a color cast. And here’s your assignment. Pick something you see every day and photograph it three different ways. A coffee mug will do just fine. It’s amazing what you start to notice when you give yourself a reason to look.” Carol Brightbill Photographer & Graphic Designer www.carolbrightbill.com

candidates.title: Why does the first scale you learn start on C? #musictheory #music #piano #majorscale #modes
candidates.description: See the two gaps in a piano's black keys? They're the reason the first scale you learn starts on C, and not A. The gaps are the only half steps on the white keys. The major scale is a pattern of whole and half steps (W W H W W W H), and its two half steps only land on the gaps one way: starting on C. That's why C major is the only major scale with no sharps or flats. So why is that note called C? The letters are older than the major scale. Roughly a thousand years ago the notes were lettered A to G from the bottom up, when music was built around D, E, F and G - the modes. The mode on C, the one we now call major, wasn't added to the list until 1547. By then, the letters were fixed. What should I explain next? candidates.title: Riemann Sum vs Integration Explained Visually | Area Under the Sine Curve #riemann #integration
candidates.description: Explore the beautiful connection between Riemann sums and definite integration through this engaging mathematical visualization of the sine function. This video demonstrates how the concept of summation gradually transforms into the idea of integration by using rectangles to approximate the area under the curve of y = sin(x) from zero to pi. Discover how the Riemann sum method works by dividing the area beneath a continuous curve into smaller rectangular sections. Each rectangle represents an approximate contribution to the total area, and the sum of these individual areas provides an estimate of the definite integral. As the number of rectangles increases, the width of each rectangle decreases, producing a more accurate approximation of the actual area. This mathematical visualization illustrates the fundamental relationship between finite sums, limits, and calculus. Watch how the number of rectangles increases progressively, making the rectangular approximation approach the smooth region beneath the sine curve. The comparison between the numerical Riemann sum and the exact value of the definite integral highlights one of the most important ideas in mathematical analysis. The definite integral of sin(x) over the interval from zero to pi equals 2. This result provides a clear example of how integration calculates the accumulated area under a function and how numerical approximation methods can approach an exact mathematical result. The visualization also introduces the midpoint Riemann sum, a numerical integration technique that uses the midpoint of each subinterval to determine the height of its corresponding rectangle. This video is ideal for students learning calculus, definite integrals, limits, numerical integration, and the mathematical foundations of area calculation. It helps make abstract mathematical concepts more intuitive by connecting graphical representations with numerical approximations and analytical results. Key mathematical concepts explored in this video include Riemann sums, definite integration, the sine function, area under a curve, midpoint approximation, limits, continuous functions, and the relationship between summation and integration. These concepts form an essential foundation for advanced calculus, mathematical modeling, physics, engineering, numerical analysis, and other scientific applications. For students preparing for mathematics examinations, competitive exams, or higher-level calculus courses, this visual explanation offers an accessible way to understand how integration emerges from the process of adding increasingly smaller contributions. Mathematics teachers can also use this example to demonstrate the connection between geometric area, numerical approximation, and exact integration. The clean visual presentation, continuously changing rectangles, and live numerical comparison make this mathematics video suitable for YouTube Shorts and other short-form educational content. It combines mathematical intuition with visual learning to make calculus more understandable, memorable, and engaging. candidates.title: What is Emotional intelligence ! #divyajain #podcast #shorts
candidates.description: What is Emotional intelligence is a question about how well we understand and manage emotions—both our own and those of other people. In psychology, emotional intelligence involves recognizing emotions accurately, understanding emotional information, using it to support thinking, and regulating emotions effectively. Emotional intelligence can influence the way we communicate, handle conflicts, build relationships and respond to difficult situations. Important aspects include self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and social awareness. It does not mean suppressing emotions or never getting angry, sad or anxious; instead, it involves recognizing what you are feeling and responding thoughtfully rather than reacting automatically. This video explores what emotional intelligence really means, how EQ differs from IQ, why understanding emotions matters in personal and professional life, and how emotional awareness can improve communication, decision-making and relationships. The discussion also looks at practical ways to develop better emotional skills in everyday situations.

candidates.description: How Was India's First Desert Cooler Invented? 😱 | The 1952 Story #Shorts #india Did you know India's first desert cooler was born from a simple summer experiment? In 1952, Ram Narayan Kher from Nagpur was tired of the extreme heat and the hassle of repeatedly wetting curtains. He decided to place an electric fan inside a wooden box lined with wood wool on three sides. When water poured over the wood wool, the fan blew out refreshing cool air! Named the "H-Desert" cooler and priced at just ₹110 back then, this genius desi invention changed summer for millions of Indian homes forever. #shorts #indianhistory #cooler #desijugaad #inventions #historyfacts #nagpur

candidates.title: Your fingers never really touch your phone…#QuantumPhysics #QuantumMechanics #Physics #Science #Mbbs
candidates.description: Your fingers never really touch your phone…#QuantumPhysics #QuantumMechanics #Physics #Science #Mbbs Have you ever wondered whether you truly touch anything? 🤯 According to quantum physics, touching is more complicated than it seems! Atoms contain nuclei surrounded by electron clouds. When your hand approaches a table, electromagnetic interactions between the atoms resist being pushed together. The Pauli exclusion principle, a fundamental quantum rule, also helps explain why ordinary matter resists compression. Your skin’s sensory receptors detect the resulting pressure and send signals to your brain, creating the sensation of touch. So, while we absolutely experience real physical contact in everyday life, the atomic explanation is far more fascinating than it appears! ⚛️ #QuantumPhysics #QuantumMechanics #Physics #Science #MindBlowingFacts #ScienceFacts #QuantumWorld #Atoms #AtomicStructure #Electrons #PauliExclusionPrinciple #ElectromagneticForce #HowThingsWork #ScienceExplained #PhysicsFacts #AmazingScience #DidYouKnow #MindBlown #InterestingFacts #ScienceEducation #LearnSomethingNew #EducationalShorts #ScienceShorts #PhysicsShorts #Universe #Reality #HumanBody #Knowledge #ExplainingMedicals #Biomedical

candidates.title: What Is a Derivative, Really? The Puzzle That Invented Calculus #calculus #maths
candidates.description: How steep is a curve at a single point? Slope needs two points -- so at one point, rise over run is 0/0. This puzzle is the entire reason calculus was invented. A straight line is easy. Take a step to the right, see how far you climb, and divide the rise by the run. On y = 1.5x that ratio is 1.5 between ANY two points. The steepness is locked in everywhere. Bend that line into the curve y = x²/2 and the single number breaks: 0.25 on the gentle left, 2.75 on the steep right, and a different value at every moment. Freeze on one point, x = 2, and ask how steep the curve is right there… and you hit a wall. With only one point there is no run and no rise: 0 divided by 0. So we cheat. Pick a second point a short step h to the right and slice a straight secant line through both. It has a real run and a real rise, so we can measure it: its slope is 2 + h/2, which is 2.5 when h = 1. But that is only the average steepness across the gap. Now slide h toward zero -- 2.3, 2.175, 2.09 … 2.0005. The secant pivots and settles onto one locked-in line: the tangent. Its slope, 2, is the derivative f′(2). 📐 THE FORMULA, READ AS AN ANIMATION f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [ f(x + h) − f(x) ] / h • h -- the tiny horizontal step between the two points (the run) • f(x + h) − f(x) -- the vertical rise between them on the curve • dividing -- the slope of the secant line • lim h → 0 -- the slope the rotating line settles into as the gap vanishes 🔍 THE BIG IDEA Zoom in close enough on any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line. The derivative is simply the slope of that line. In the video, y = x²/2 is magnified a thousand times around x = 2, and the curve that bowed across the whole screen becomes a straight line of slope 2. 📌 IN THIS VIDEO • Slope as rise over run, and why a straight line needs only one number • Why a curve's steepness changes from point to point • Why "steepness at one point" gives 0/0 • Secant lines: the average slope across a gap • Shrinking h to zero: the secant turns into the tangent • The derivative as the slope of the tangent line • The limit definition of the derivative, piece by piece • Local linearity: every smooth curve is straight up close ⏱ CHAPTERS 0:00 How steep is a curve at ONE point? 0:18 A straight line: rise over run 0:36 Bend it into a curve -- the slope breaks 0:52 One point, a wall: 0/0 1:16 The cheat: a second point 1:29 The secant line (average slope) 1:47 Slide h to zero 2:08 The tangent line 2:26 That number is the derivative 2:42 The formula is a recipe 3:06 Zoom in: every curve is straight 🎨 COLOUR KEY Yellow = the run and the step h · Blue = the curve and the rise · Green = every slope (secant, tangent, derivative) · Red = 0/0 🧠 TRY IT YOURSELF Run the recipe on the video's curve, f(x) = x²/2. Show that the secant slope is x + h/2, so the derivative at ANY point is just x. Then check the magnifying lens near the end: when it slides to x = 2.7, what slope should the straight line inside read? And using the same recipe (not the power rule), what is the slope of y = x² at x = 3? Answer in the comments 👇 📚 FURTHER WATCHING & READING • 3Blue1Brown, "The paradox of the derivative" -- Essence of Calculus, Chapter 2 (this film's colours follow its conventions: yellow for the run, blue for the rise, green for the slope) • Silvanus P. Thompson, Calculus Made Easy (1910) • Gilbert Strang, Calculus, Chapter 2: Derivatives (free on MIT OpenCourseWare) 🎬 Animated in 3D with ManimGL. Every number on screen is computed and checked. #Calculus #Derivative #Mathematics #Maths #Limits #MathAnimation #STEM

candidates.title: You Have NEVER Actually Touched Anything! 🤯⚛️ #QuantumPhysics #ScientificFacts #SciFlo #science
candidates.description: Have you ever wondered if you have REALLY touched anything in your entire life? 🤯 According to quantum physics, the reality of touch is far stranger than you might imagine! When you touch another person, hold your phone, or place your hand against a wall, the atoms in your body don’t simply collide like tiny solid objects. Instead, something fascinating happens at the atomic level. ⚛️ THE SCIENCE BEHIND TOUCH 1. Atoms: Everything around you, including your body, is made of atoms. 2. Electrons: Atoms contain negatively charged electrons surrounding their nuclei. 3. Electromagnetic Repulsion: When atoms approach one another, electromagnetic interactions between their electrons strongly resist further compression. 4. Pauli Exclusion Principle: This quantum mechanical principle also helps prevent electrons from occupying identical quantum states. 5. The Sensation of Touch: Your nervous system detects forces and pressure through specialized receptors in your skin, allowing your brain to experience the sensation of touching something. 6. The Quantum Reality: What feels like physical contact is actually the result of complex electromagnetic and quantum interactions between matter. So, when you shake someone’s hand, touch a wall, or hold your phone, you’re experiencing forces between atoms rather than tiny solid surfaces simply meeting. IMPORTANT SCIENTIFIC FACT: Saying that you never touch anything is a simplified way of describing atomic interactions. It doesn’t mean physical contact is imaginary or that atoms never interact. At first glance it is just a portrait of an old man with a staff, standing against the sea. Then you mirror the canvas down the middle. Take the right half and mirror it: the fisherman is praying, eyes closed, hands at rest. Take the left half and mirror it: the face turns into a horned demon, staring straight back at you. Same paint. Same face. Two completely different people. In this Short we look at the hidden details in this painting — the symmetry trick Csontváry built into the composition, the two faces hiding in one canvas, and why the artist painted it at all. Ink & Instinct is where famous paintings explained meets the strange details nobody points out — art mysteries, symbolism and hidden meanings inside historic artworks. candidates.title: Why Is This Country Inside Another Country? 🌍 #geography #shorts #facts
candidates.description: Why does a tiny country cut almost 500 km through another country? 🌍😳 Look at the map of Africa. Senegal is almost split by a narrow, snake-shaped country called The Gambia. But why does this bizarre border exist? The answer takes us back to a fierce colonial rivalry between Britain and France. In 1889, the two empires negotiated boundaries around the strategically important Gambia River, creating one of Africa's most unusual country shapes. Discover how geography, colonial history, and a single river shaped the map of West Africa! 💬 What other strange borders should we explore next? Comment below! Why does a thin strip of land cut through Senegal? Discover the history behind the unusual Senegal Gambia border. 🌍 The Gambia is essentially a long, narrow enclave surrounded by Senegal on three sides, with the Atlantic Ocean to the west. This strange layout is the result of colonial-era negotiations between Britain and France in 1889. The two powers drew borders based on the Gambia River, which served as a crucial trade route for the British at the time. By tracing the river’s path, the colonial powers created one of the most distinct map anomalies in West Africa. Understanding how this border was formed offers a clear look at how historical trade interests continue to shape modern national boundaries. These geography facts highlight how colonial decisions still influence the world map today. candidates.title: How A Wankel Rotary Engine Works⚙️ #physics #automobile #engineering #pixelart #engineeringexplained
candidates.description: *The following figures are for a typical twin-rotor Wankel engine.* Unlike a conventional piston engine, a rotary engine uses triangular rotors spinning inside specially shaped housings to produce power. Each rotor creates three separate chambers, which continuously go through four stages: 1. Intake: Air and fuel enter the chamber. 2. Compression: The mixture is compressed. 3. Combustion: Spark plugs ignite the mixture, pushing the rotor and producing power. 4. Exhaust: The burnt gases are expelled. All four stages happen simultaneously, but in different chambers! And here's the crazy part: 🔥 At 9,000 RPM, a twin-rotor engine produces approximately 300 combustion events per second! 🔥 Even at 1,000 RPM idle, that's around 33 combustion events per second! A fascinating piece of engineering that produces power in a completely different way. *The sound is an illustrative recreation, not an actual recording of a specific car or engine.* **Sources:** - Mazda – Rotary Engine Technical Information - Haynes Manuals – Guide to Rotary Engines - MDPI – Two-Stroke Wankel Type Rotary Engine (2019) #RotaryEngine #Engineering #Automotive #Mechanics #8BitEngineering

candidates.title: Understanding Emotional Intelligence
candidates.description: His IQ was fine. Picking between two dates took him 30 minutes. 🗓️ Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio studied patients whose reasoning survived brain damage but whose feelings went flat. He offered one of them two dates for a visit. The man weighed pros and cons, other plans, even the weather. After about 30 minutes, Damasio just picked one for him. "Fine," the man said. Feelings aren't the enemy of thinking. They're how you choose. Emotional intelligence is reading and steering them, both yours and other people's. Here are 3 moves to train it: 🏷️ 1. Name it: UCLA psychologists had 88 people who were afraid of spiders walk up to a live tarantula. One group said their fear out loud: "I'm terrified of that nasty spider." A week later, with a new spider, their hands sweated the least. Naming a feeling doesn't feed it. It turns it down. So get specific: not "bad," but anxious, embarrassed or left out. ❓ 2. Ask, don't guess: Researchers asked couples who'd been together about 10 years to predict each other's answers. The ones who first imagined being in their partner's shoes did slightly worse, while feeling more confident. Across 25 experiments, imagining never reliably helped. Asking did. Empathy isn't mind reading. It's a good question, and then actually listening. 🔁 3. Reframe: Over 90% of people say the best advice before a stressful task is "calm down." A Harvard researcher tested that with karaoke. Singers who first said "I am excited" out loud scored about 80% accuracy. Singers who said "I am anxious" scored about 53%. So don't fight the pounding heart. Relabel it: "I'm excited." Plot twist: the famous claim that emotional intelligence matters twice as much as IQ comes from a 1998 business bestseller, and researchers have pushed back on it ever since. EQ does predict job performance, mostly in emotionally heavy jobs, but it's not a second IQ. It's a set of skills. Name what you feel. Ask what they feel. Reframe what your body is telling you. 📤 Send this to someone who says they don't do feelings. Then ask them how that makes them feel. 🔔 Subscribe to Think Sharper for short lessons on how to learn faster and think smarter. #emotionalintelligence #psychology #thinksharper #shorts #eq #mentalhealth #selfimprovement #communication #empathy #anxiety #mindset #relationships

candidates.title: Planck's Constant Is the Twin of the Speed of Light | Understanding Quantum Mechanics from Geometry
candidates.description: An educational physics video narrated by David Charles — author of Understanding Quantum Mechanics through Geometry and the Geometric Truth series. This short explains, in detail, what Planck's constant actually is and where it comes from. For 125 years h has been treated as a brute fact — a number you measure but never explain. Here it is derived, step by step, from the geometry of the hydrogen atom. What the video covers: - The conjugate pair. Planck's constant (h) and the speed of light (c) are two faces of one atom — c read from the atom's length (its Lyman wavelength), h read from its energy (the ground state, 13.6 eV). - The derivation of Planck's constant: h = (π/180)² × (1 + α/2π)⁻² × 10⁻¹² × E_Ly — one "square degree" of the hydrogen circle's energy, with a small fine-structure adjustment, delivered once per turn. - The cancellation. The same machinery sits on both constants, inverted; multiply c and h and every piece cancels, leaving E·λ = hc — hydrogen's two faces. - Why QM becomes intelligible: energy leaves in whole packets, once per turn, so quantum numbers are counts of whole turns. Quantum mechanics isn't a mystery — it's a circle that turns. Who it's for: science students, science teachers, university lecturers and professors, researchers, and the intelligent, curious public — anyone who'd rather see where a fundamental constant comes from than accept it as given. From Volume 5 — Understanding Quantum Mechanics through Geometry, by David Charles, part of the Geometric Truth series. Read more at thegeometrictruth.com The full derivation is in the book. 📖 GO DEEPER — THE WEBSITE AND THE BOOK 🌐 The website — the full theory, every proof, and the whole series in one place: https://thegeometrictruth.com 📙 The book — Volume 5 of the Geometric Truth series, by David Charles: "Understanding Quantum Mechanics through Geometry" — available on Amazon in paperback and Kindle (search "QM from Geometry David Charles"), or follow the links at https://thegeometrictruth.com Hashtags #physics #quantummechanics #planckconstant #speedoflight #hydrogenatom #finestructureconstant #geometry #physicseducation #quantumphysics #science #scienceeducation #physicsteacher #STEM #shorts

candidates.title: How to Build a Tank, One Problem at a Time 🪖 #shorts
candidates.description: Bolt steel plates onto a farm tractor and you are one problem away from the next part. Mud, trenches, a gun that only points one way, an engine that cooks the crew, no radio, and tea. Every part of a tank exists because something went wrong first. Why are tracks called caterpillar tracks? Why was the first tank shaped like a rhombus? Why do British tanks have a kettle built in? And why is it called a "tank" at all? Facts in this short: • The British Army asked for a machine that could cross a trench 8 feet wide. That is why the first tanks (1916) had tracks running all the way around a rhomboid hull. • Inside the Mark I the crew shared one space with the engine: up to 122 °F (50 °C), exhaust fumes, and men passing out. • The Renault FT (1917) put the gun in a fully rotating turret and the engine in its own compartment at the back. Almost every tank since has copied that layout. • Early tanks had no radio. Crews carried two carrier pigeons. • Since the Centurion (1945), British tanks carry a built-in boiling vessel for hot water, rations and tea. • In 1915 the secret machines were described as "water carriers for Mesopotamia". The code name stuck: tank. #engineering #tank #history #howitworks #ww1 #science #shorts

Born around 470 BCE in Athens, Socrates became famous for questioning assumptions, challenging people to think deeply, and encouraging self-examination. He left no known writings of his own; much of what we know about him comes through later writers, especially Plato and Xenophon. Two ideas traditionally associated with Socrates are featured in this video: 1. “The only true wisdom is in knowing that you know nothing.” 2. “An unexamined life is not worth living.” These ideas highlight intellectual humility, critical thinking, self-awareness, ethical living, and the importance of questioning our beliefs. His Socratic method—asking careful questions rather than simply giving answers—continues to influence education, philosophy, law, science, and critical thinking. candidates.title: Every note secretly contains a chord. #musictheory #music #piano #physics #harmonics
candidates.description: Every note you play is secretly a chord. A string doesn't only swing as a whole - it also swings in halves, thirds and quarters, all at once. These are its harmonics. Harmonics 4, 5 and 6 are C, E and G: a major chord inside a single note. Try it on any acoustic piano: silently hold down C, E and G, strike a low C and let go - they ring on their own (sympathetic resonance). How loud each harmonic is gives a note its timbre, which is why a cello, a saxophone and a piano playing the same C all sound different. And your brain is so used to the pattern that it fills in the bottom note when it's missing. What should I explain next? Tell me in the comments. Piano sample: Salamander Grand Piano by Alexander Holm (CC BY 3.0). Saxophone: "Sax Alto - C4" by MTG, freesound.org (CC BY 3.0). Cello: University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios. #musictheory #music #physics #piano #shorts

candidates.description: The Mistake That Invented the Matchstick! 😱🔥 #shorts #history Did you know the matchstick was invented completely by accident? In 1826, British chemist John Walker was stirring chemicals with a wooden stick when a dry lump formed on its tip. When he scraped it against the floor to clean it, it instantly burst into flames! That simple mistake gave birth to friction matches. However, early matches carried a dark secret: dangerous white phosphorus caused a severe disease called "Phossy Jaw" among factory workers. Discover how a crucial switch to red phosphorus gave us the modern safety match we use today! 🔔 Subscribe to Indian Story Wala Shorts for more incredible history, untold stories, and fascinating science facts! #shorts #history #invention #matchstick #didyouknow #sciencefacts #facts #shortsvideo invention of matchstick, how matches were invented, accidental inventions, john walker chemist, history of matches, safety match history, phossy jaw disease, white phosphorus matchsticks, red phosphorus safety match, untold history facts, amazing science facts, crazy history facts, history shorts, did you know facts, everyday science, viral shorts, indian story wala shorts

candidates.description: ! 🌿 प्रकृति की दुनिया में ऐसे कई पौधे हैं जिनकी जीवन शैली किसी चमत्कार से कम नहीं। अमेज़न (Amazon) के शांत तालाबों और नदियों में पाया जाने वाला यह अद्भुत लैवेंडर फूल (Water Hyacinth / जलकुंभी) अपनी पीढ़ी को आगे बढ़ाने के लिए एक बेहद अनोखी रणनीति अपनाता है! candidates.title: Disney Built Its Castle Too Short😳
candidates.description: Disney's Cinderella Castle stops at 189 feet. Just 11 feet short of a rule that would have ruined it. 🏰 The section: • In the US, the FAA generally requires structures taller than 200 feet to carry obstruction lighting, the flashing red lights that warn pilots. • Cinderella Castle (Magic Kingdom, 1971) was kept at 189 feet (57.6 m), so no warning lights on top. • To make it feel taller, the designers used forced perspective: windows, doors and stonework get smaller the higher you go. • Your brain reads "smaller" as "further away", so the top looks much higher than it really is. • Main Street, U.S.A. uses the same trick on its upper floors. Fair point: the 200-foot rule isn't the only reason. Forced perspective is a classic Disney design tool, and they use it all over the parks. Clever design 🧠 or cheap trick 🎭? candidates.title: How Ancient Sand DROPPED A 15-Ton Stone Wall ⛏️🚪 #shorts
candidates.description: Ancient tomb builders didn’t use cranes or winches to seal this underground passage—they used gravity and dry desert sand. ⛏️🚪 Inside the Great Pyramid of Giza, three massive red granite blocks weighing roughly 5 tons each were balanced directly above a steep 26-degree incline. Instead of lifting this 15-ton stone wall, engineers placed them on tightly packed chambers of fine quartz sand. When workers pulled the drainage plugs, the sand flowed out like a giant hourglass. As the chambers emptied, the 15-ton granite wall slid down the slope and permanently jammed the entrance shut from the inside. ⏳🔒 🔍 Inside this breakdown: • The 26-degree slope of the Great Pyramid's Ascending Passage. • How 3 massive granite plugs were balanced on fine sand. • The hourglass drainage system that triggered the release. • Why ancient intruders in 820 AD couldn't budge the stones and had to chisel through solid rock around them. 📌 Primary Archaeological References: • Sir William Matthew Flinders Petrie, "The Pyramids and Temples of Gizeh" (1883) • Dr. Mark Lehner, "The Complete Pyramids" (Thames & Hudson, 1997) • Georges Goyon, "Les secrets des bâtisseurs des grandes pyramides" #shorts #ancienthistory #engineering #ValueMatrix #pyramids #didyouknow #factshorts #ancientdiscoveries

candidates.title: How Did Romans Turn Water Into Flour 2,000 Years Ago? #shorts
candidates.description: A waterwheel turns upright, but a millstone spins flat. So how did the Romans connect them? 🤔 Hidden inside every ancient Roman watermill was a clever wooden gear system. A cog wheel on the waterwheel's axle meshed with a lantern pinion, turning the motion ninety degrees and speeding it up like a bicycle in high gear. The vertical shaft then locked into the runner stone, spinning it against the fixed lower stone to shear grain into flour. No engines. No electricity. Just flowing water and simple wooden gears. 👉 Follow for more hidden engineering secrets from the ancient world! #Shorts #RomanEngineering #AncientEngineering #Watermill #Archaeology #HistoryFacts #HowItWorks #Engineering

candidates.title: Bharata's Padukas | 3 Leadership Lessons from Ramayana for Project Managers #shorts
candidates.description: 🏹 WHAT HAPPENS TO YOUR PROJECT WHEN THE LEADER IS AWAY? Does work continue smoothly—or do important decisions pile up? The story of Bharata's Padukas from the Ramayana offers a powerful lesson about delegation, authority, and responsible leadership. Welcome to Episode 02 of Ramayana × Project Management by PMO Wisdom! 🎯 TODAY'S STORY: BHARATA'S PADUKAS When Rama was in exile, Bharata placed Rama's sandals (Padukas) on the throne and governed in his name for fourteen years. Bharata's actions symbolised his commitment to Rama's rightful authority and his responsibility to serve as a steward. What can project managers learn from this story? ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 1: MAKE AUTHORITY VISIBLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Everyone should know who has the authority to make decisions. In project management, unclear decision rights can create delays, confusion, and unnecessary escalation. Before a planned absence, clarify: ✅ Who can make routine decisions ✅ Which decisions require escalation ✅ What approval limits apply ✅ Who communicates important decisions A project should not stop simply because one person is unavailable. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 2: ACT AS A STEWARD, NOT AN OWNER ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Bharata governed in Rama's name rather than claiming the throne as his own. In project management, delegated authority should be exercised responsibly. A project manager or deputy should: • Respect the sponsor's intent • Work within agreed decision limits • Protect the project's objectives • Remain accountable for decisions made Leadership is about serving the agreed purpose, not treating delegated authority as personal power. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 📘 LESSON 3: HAND BACK CLEANLY ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Delegation should include a clear process for handing responsibility back. Maintain: ✅ A transparent decision log ✅ Records of important approvals ✅ A list of unresolved issues ✅ Clear communication about changes When the original leader returns, they should be able to understand what happened and resume responsibility without confusion. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 💡 PRACTICAL PROJECT EXAMPLE ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Imagine a project manager takes three weeks of leave. BEFORE: ❌ 40 decisions are waiting ❌ Nobody knows who can approve what ❌ Progress slows down AFTER: ✅ A deputy is appointed ✅ Decision limits are defined ✅ A decision log is maintained ✅ The project keeps moving The difference is not the absence of the leader. It is the clarity of delegated authority. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ⚠️ MISTAKE TO AVOID ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Leaving a project without clear delegation. When nobody knows who can decide, even small issues may remain unresolved. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎯 TRY THIS IN YOUR NEXT PROJECT ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Before your next planned absence: 1️⃣ Identify your deputy. 2️⃣ Define their decision-making authority. 3️⃣ Agree on escalation limits. 4️⃣ Establish a decision log and handback process. Ask yourself: "Who covers for me when I'm away?" 💡 KEY TAKEAWAY MAKE AUTHORITY VISIBLE. ACT AS A STEWARD. HAND BACK CLEANLY. Strong governance allows work to continue while preserving accountability. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 🎬 RAMAYANA × PROJECT MANAGEMENT ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Episode 02/12 — Bharata's Padukas NEXT EPISODE: Episode 03 — Jatayu's Warning Explore timeless stories from the Ramayana and their practical connections with leadership, project governance, decision-making, and stakeholder management. 📺 Subscribe to PMO Wisdom: https://youtube.com/@PMOWisdom One Topic. candidates.title: The Universe Has a Measurement Crisis (Scientists Can’t Agree) 🌌
candidates.description: The universe is expanding, but nobody can agree on how fast. And that disagreement might be the biggest crisis in modern physics. 🌌 In this Short from Cosmic Series, we explore the Hubble Tension: two precise measurements of the same thing, giving two different answers. Both claim to be right. Both can’t be. 🔭 WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS SHORT: ✅ What the Hubble constant is and why it tells us how fast the universe is expanding today. ✅ The two completely different ways scientists measure it: the “local ladder” of pulsating stars and exploding stars, and the “early universe” method that uses the leftover glow of the Big Bang. ✅ Why the local method gives about 73 kilometers per second per megaparsec, while the early universe method gives about 67 to 68. ✅ Why some scientists now call it the Hubble Crisis instead of the Hubble Tension. ✅ How the James Webb Space Telescope re-checked the measurements, and what it found. ✅ Why one respected team, using a different type of star, gets a value in the middle, and why that keeps the controversy alive. ✅ What it could mean for physics if the tension is real: new kinds of dark energy, new particles, or even a change in our understanding of gravity. 🌠 WHAT IS THE HUBBLE CONSTANT? In 1929, Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster they move. The Hubble constant is the number that describes this rate. A value of 70 means that a galaxy 3.3 million light-years away is receding at about 70 kilometers per second, and a galaxy ten times farther is receding ten times faster. It is one of the most important numbers in cosmology, because it sets the age, size, and fate of the universe. 📏 TWO RULERS, TWO ANSWERS Ruler number one looks at the nearby universe. Astronomers measure the distances to pulsating stars called Cepheids, red giant stars, and exploding stars called supernovae, and build a “distance ladder” step by step. The most recent combined results of this method give a value of about 73.5. Ruler number two looks at the oldest light in the cosmos, the cosmic microwave background, which was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Using our standard model of cosmology, scientists calculate what the expansion rate should be today. That calculation gives about 67 to 68. The difference between the two is far too large to be a simple coincidence. Some studies put it at roughly five to seven standard deviations, which is the level where scientists stop calling it a fluke. 🧪 IS IT JUST A MEASUREMENT ERROR? That was the first suspect. But the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope have looked at the same stars again with sharper vision, and the tension did not go away. Many researchers now say that a single overlooked mistake is very unlikely to explain it. Still, the debate is far from over. Another team, using a different kind of star as its distance marker, finds a value of around 70, right between the two camps, and argues that the problem may be smaller than it looks. This is real, honest science: careful measurements, strong disagreement, and no final verdict yet. 💡 WHY THIS MATTERS If the tension is real, our standard model of the universe may be missing something important. Ideas being studied include early dark energy, extra types of particles, interactions between dark matter and dark energy, and changes to gravity. If it is not real, then we may have misunderstood one of our own measuring tools. Either way, we learn something big. 🔮 WHAT COMES NEXT? New data from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Euclid mission, the DESI survey, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, along with gravitational waves and gravitational lensing, will test both rulers with new methods. Within the next few years, we may finally know which one is wrong, or whether the universe is hiding something new. 🌙 COMING SOON ON COSMIC SERIES A full tour of the Moon is on its way. candidates.title: The Unit Circle Explained 🔵 | Sine, Cosine, Angles & Trigonometry #mathshorts #unitcircle #maths
candidates.description: Explore the beauty of the unit circle through a clear, colorful, and dynamic mathematical visualization. This video from codematrixvishal explains the fundamental concepts of the unit circle and demonstrates the relationship between angles, sine, cosine, coordinates, and trigonometric identities. The unit circle is one of the most important concepts in trigonometry. It is a circle with a radius of one unit centered at the origin of the coordinate plane. Every point on the circumference represents a pair of coordinates determined by an angle measured from the positive x-axis. These coordinates are expressed as (cos θ, sin θ), connecting circular motion with the fundamental trigonometric functions. This mathematical visualization illustrates how a point moves around the unit circle through a complete 360-degree rotation. As the angle changes, the horizontal coordinate represents cos θ, while the vertical coordinate represents sin θ. These changing values demonstrate how sine and cosine depend on the angle and how their values vary throughout the four quadrants of the coordinate plane. The visualization highlights the radius, coordinate axes, angle theta, moving point P, horizontal cosine component, and vertical sine component. The right-triangle relationship between these components provides an intuitive understanding of the connection between geometry and trigonometry. The radius remains equal to one throughout the rotation, leading to the fundamental trigonometric identity: cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 This identity is one of the most widely used relationships in mathematics. It plays an essential role in simplifying trigonometric expressions, solving equations, studying periodic functions, analyzing circular motion, and understanding advanced mathematical concepts. The unit circle also provides a geometric foundation for understanding positive and negative trigonometric values across different quadrants. It connects coordinate geometry, angles, circular motion, periodicity, and the behavior of sine and cosine functions in a single mathematical framework. This video is useful for students studying school mathematics, trigonometry, coordinate geometry, higher mathematics, calculus, and mathematical analysis. It provides a visual learning experience for understanding the unit circle, the meaning of trigonometric coordinates, the relationship between sine and cosine, and the importance of fundamental trigonometric identities. Whether you are revising essential trigonometry concepts, strengthening your mathematical foundation, preparing for examinations, or exploring the visual side of mathematics, this unit circle animation offers a simple and engaging way to understand these important relationships. candidates.title: Quantum Model of the Atom: Why Atoms Don't Collapse
candidates.description: The quantum model of the atom: why atoms don't collapse If electrons orbited the nucleus like planets, the circling charge would give off light, lose energy and spiral in. Every atom would collapse in about 16 trillionths of a second. But an electron isn't a tiny ball. It's a wave, and a trapped wave can only take certain shapes, like a string's notes or a drum's patterns. Around a nucleus those patterns are three-dimensional: the orbitals 1s, 2s, 2p and 3d. Squeeze the wave tighter and its energy rises, so the lowest pattern is a floor the electron can't fall through: −13.6 eV, at 0.053 nm. An orbital isn't a path. Look once and the electron is at one spot; look thousands of times and the dots build the cloud. Each orbital holds 2 electrons, and they come in families of 1, 3, 5 and 7. That makes 2, 6, 10 and 14: the widths of the s, p, d and f blocks of the periodic table. #facts #education #study #student #learning #science #chemistry #physics #quantum #quantumphysics #quantummechanics #physicsfun #periodictable #chemistryclass #chemistrystudent

candidates.title: The Softest Tool Cut the Hardest Stone  Ancient Egypt 3D Short
candidates.description: The softest tool cut the hardest stone. Five thousand years ago, Egyptian craftsmen carved flawless vases from diorite — one of the hardest stones on earth — with tools made of copper, one of the softest metals. Copper alone could never cut diorite. The real cutter was sand: quartz grains trapped in the soft copper edge, turning it into thousands of tiny teeth that ground the stone away, turn by turn. This 3D short shows the whole chain — the sand, the trapped grains, the weighted drill, the narrow neck widened from inside, the polishing, the quarry, and the finished vases — with the inside of each step shown, so you can see how it works.

candidates.title: Shoes before socks? | Topological Sort #Shorts
candidates.description: 1. Why it matters: shoes first, then socks? It doesn't work. Some things must come before others, and a school with fifty courses, each needing others first, can't be planned by guessing. 2. What it is: topological sort lines everything up so every arrow points forward, never backward. Like a recipe: chop before you fry, fry before you serve. 3. How it works: six things to wear. Count the arrows coming in to each one. Socks, pants and shirt have zero, so they're free. Put a free one in line, erase its arrows, and repeat: socks, pants, shoes, shirt, belt, jacket. Every arrow points forward. If the arrows form a loop, nothing ever reaches zero, so no order exists. 4. Where it's used: planning school courses (algebra, then calculus, then physics) and spreadsheets, which update dependent cells in the right order. 5. In short: count the arrows coming in, take what's free, and line everything up with arrows pointing forward. Following the table of contents of CLRS "Introduction to Algorithms", one algorithm a day, explained at a high-school level. Visuals and animation are generated with code; the narration is an AI clone of my own voice. #algorithms #computerscience #topologicalsort #graphs #dag #learntocode #shorts

candidates.title: What Is the Real Meaning of Opportunity Cost in Economics? #interview #economics
candidates.description: What is opportunity cost in economics, and how do you identify the best alternative when every option costs the same? This simple ₹10 question about apples, bananas, and oranges reveals an important lesson in economics, business management, decision-making, and leadership. In this MBAyogaGuru discussion, Prof. VKJ challenges a candidate to explain the opportunity cost of buying an apple when two bananas and two oranges are available for the same price. The conversation highlights why knowing the definition of opportunity cost is not enough. You must also understand the criteria used to evaluate alternatives and determine which option offers the highest value. What Is Opportunity Cost? Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative that you give up when you make a choice. When you have limited resources, such as money, time, or effort, every decision involves choosing one option over another. The opportunity cost depends on the value of the best alternative forgone, not simply on the price of the item you purchase. Through this practical example, Prof. VKJ explains how personal needs, priorities, and decision-making criteria can influence the value of different alternatives. The discussion also connects opportunity cost to leadership, critical thinking, problem-solving, and business decision-making. This concept is especially useful for MBA students, management aspirants, CA and CMA candidates, economics students, business professionals, and anyone preparing for management interviews or competitive examinations. Can you answer the question? If you spend ₹10 on an apple, what is your opportunity cost, and how would you decide between two bananas and two oranges? Share your reasoning in the comments. candidates.title: Network Topology Explained 🌐 | Star, Bus, Ring, Mesh & Tree #Shorts
candidates.description: 🌐 Network Topology Explained Network topology describes the arrangement of devices and connections inside a computer network. In this Tech Shortcut, learn five common network topologies: ⭐ Star Topology All devices connect to a central device such as a switch. 🚌 Bus Topology Devices share a single main communication cable or backbone. 🔄 Ring Topology Devices are connected in a circular path. 🕸️ Mesh Topology Devices are connected through multiple paths, providing greater redundancy. 🌳 Tree Topology A hierarchical structure that combines characteristics of multiple network arrangements, often resembling interconnected star networks. Quick revision: Star → Central Device Bus → Single Backbone Ring → Circular Path Mesh → Multiple Paths Tree → Hierarchical Structure 📌 The best topology depends on factors such as cost, reliability, scalability, performance and network requirements. 💡 Save this Short as your quick Network Topology cheat sheet. candidates.title: बल्ब का आविष्कार किसने किया? Edison vs Joseph Swan की कहानी
candidates.description: आज Electric Bulb हर घर की सबसे आम चीज़ है, लेकिन इसके आविष्कार का श्रेय सिर्फ़ Thomas Edison को देना अधूरी कहानी है। Bulb का आविष्कार किसने किया: Edison ने या Joseph Swan ने? अक्टूबर 1879 में अमेरिका के New Jersey के Menlo Park में Thomas Edison अपनी lab में एक छोटी सी problem से जूझ रहे थे। बल्ब जलते तो थे, लेकिन ज़्यादा देर नहीं टिकते थे। उस दौर में शहर गैस की लालटेनों से रोशन होते थे। असली अड़चन filament की थी। उसे तेज़ गर्मी सहनी थी, उसका resistance ज़्यादा होना चाहिए था ताकि कई बल्ब एक साथ जुड़ सकें, और काँच के अंदर की हवा लगभग पूरी निकालनी थी। एक साल से ज़्यादा की नाकामियों के बाद Edison की टीम ने carbon में बदला हुआ सूती सिलाई का धागा आज़माया। बल्ब करीब साढ़े 13 घंटे जलता रहा और उसकी रोशनी करीब 33 मोमबत्तियों के बराबर थी। आगे चलकर carbonized bamboo के filament से Edison के बल्ब 1200 घंटे से ज़्यादा जलने लगे। लेकिन Edison अकेले नहीं थे। इंग्लैंड के Newcastle में Joseph Swan भी यही कोशिश कर रहे थे। उनकी ताकत vacuum pump थी, जिस पर वे 1877 में ही patent ले चुके थे। 18 दिसंबर 1878 को, यानी Edison की कामयाबी से करीब 10 महीने पहले, Swan ने carbon filament वाला बल्ब सबके सामने जलाकर दिखाया, लेकिन वह कुछ ही मिनटों में टूट गया। फरवरी 1879 में उन्होंने 700 से ज़्यादा लोगों के सामने दोबारा demonstration किया। नवंबर 1879 में Edison ने अपना patent आवेदन दिया। 31 दिसंबर 1879 को Menlo Park में पहला public demonstration हुआ, जिसके लिए Pennsylvania Railroad ने उस शाम खास ट्रेन चलाई। 27 जनवरी 1880 को Edison को अमेरिका में patent मिल गया। ब्रिटेन में कहानी उलटी निकली। वहाँ Swan को 1880 में patent मिला, जबकि Edison का आवेदन नाकाम रहा। 1881 में लंदन का Savoy Theatre Swan के करीब 1200 बल्बों से जगमगाया और पूरी तरह बिजली से रोशन होने वाली दुनिया की पहली public building बना। मुकदमों में उलझने की जगह दोनों ने हाथ मिलाना चुना। 1883 में उनकी कंपनियाँ मिलकर Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company बन गईं, और नई कंपनी के बल्बों में Swan का बनाया filament इस्तेमाल हुआ। Electric Bulb Reference Image Credit: [Source] Photo by: [Name] candidates.title: Wisdom is knowing which battles deserve your strength. #philosophy #quotes
candidates.description: Sun Tzu, traditionally (544–496 BC), was an ancient Chinese military strategist and philosopher. He is traditionally credited as the author of The Art of War, a classic work on strategy and conflict. His teachings emphasize preparation, discipline, adaptability, and understanding human behavior. The historical details of his life remain uncertain, and some scholars question whether he was a single historical person. His ideas have influenced military leaders, political thinkers, and business strategists for centuries. The Art of War teaches that winning does not always require fighting. Sun Tzu argues that a wise commander studies both the opponent and himself before choosing a battle. He values timing, patience, and strategic judgment over reckless aggression. His philosophy suggests that knowing when to avoid conflict can be as important as knowing how to win it. That principle closely matches the meaning of your quote. Sun Tzu’s legacy rests on the idea that strength without judgment can become a weakness. His work continues to be studied in military history, leadership, strategy, and philosophy. Text - A man who knows how to battle will win many battles, but a man who knows when to battle will not lose a single one. - @ORSELION-n3m #philosophy #lifelessons #deepthoughts #truth #reality #lifequotes #humannature #quotes #history

candidates.description: क्या आप जानते हैं कि एक ऐसा इंजन बनाया गया था, जो पेट्रोल या डीजल के बजाय वनस्पति तेल पर भी चल सकता था? इस अनोखे आविष्कार के पीछे थे जर्मन इंजीनियर Rudolf Diesel, जिन्होंने एक ऐसी मशीन बनाने का सपना देखा था, जो कम ईंधन में ज्यादा ताकत पैदा कर सके। साल 1892 में उन्होंने अपने नए इंजन का पेटेंट आवेदन किया। लेकिन इस इंजन को बनाना बिल्कुल आसान नहीं था। शुरुआती प्रयोगों में कई बार विस्फोट हुए और रुडोल्फ डीजल की जान तक खतरे में पड़ गई। उनका इंजन दूसरे इंजनों से बिल्कुल अलग तरीके से काम करता था। इसमें स्पार्क प्लग की जरूरत नहीं थी। पहले सिलेंडर के अंदर हवा को बहुत ज्यादा दबाया जाता था, जिससे उसका तापमान बढ़ जाता था। फिर उसमें ईंधन डाला जाता, जो गर्म हवा के संपर्क में आते ही अपने आप जलने लगता था। कई वर्षों की मेहनत और तकनीकी सुधारों के बाद 28 जनवरी 1897 को पहला सफल व्यावहारिक डीजल इंजन तैयार हुआ। लेकिन इस आविष्कार की सबसे दिलचस्प बात अभी बाकी थी! साल 1900 में पेरिस विश्व प्रदर्शनी में डीजल इंजन को मूंगफली के तेल से चलाकर भी दिखाया गया। इससे साबित हुआ कि इस इंजन में केवल पेट्रोलियम ईंधन का इस्तेमाल करना जरूरी नहीं था। आगे चलकर इसी तकनीक ने ट्रकों, जहाजों, ट्रेनों और भारी मशीनों की दुनिया बदल दी। लेकिन इस महान आविष्कारक का अंत बेहद रहस्यमयी रहा। 1913 में इंग्लैंड जाते समय Rudolf Diesel जहाज से अचानक लापता हो गए और कुछ दिनों बाद समुद्र में उनका शव मिला। आखिर जिस इंजीनियर ने दुनिया को एक नई इंजन तकनीक दी, उसकी मौत के पीछे क्या रहस्य छिपा था? candidates.title: these spinning circles are drawing a bass clef 🎼
candidates.description: The outline of a bass clef, sampled at 2048 points, is a sum of spinning circles: z(t) = ∑ cₖ eⁱᵏᵗ, with the cₖ from its discrete Fourier transform. Circle k has radius |cₖ| and turns k times per lap. Keep only the N biggest circles and the widest gap to the outline is 35.3% of the bass clef's height at N = 2, 12.1% at N = 8, 2.2% at N = 32, 0.49% at N = 128 and just 0.12% at N = 512. The two dots are separate shapes, so the circles draw the clef as one continuous line and hop across to each dot and back: the short straight strokes are those hops. The sound is built the same way: an F (the note the bass clef is named after) with more overtones added every time more circles join. candidates.title: BrahMos: Mach 3 Cruise Missile!
candidates.description: BrahMos is one of the fastest cruise missiles in operation, flying at about three times the speed of sound. In this short Hindi-narrated video, we explain how this India-Russia missile works, in simple words and without the hype. BrahMos is a joint India-Russia project, and it can be launched from land, ships, submarines or aircraft. It flies at about Mach 2.8 to 3, which is around 3,700 km/h. What you will learn: • Why BrahMos is counted among the fastest operational cruise missiles • How the India-Russia project works, and from which platforms it can be launched • The warhead: officially conventional, about 200 kg, and up to 300 kg in the air-launched version • The two stages: a solid booster takes it to supersonic speed and separates, then a liquid ramjet engine keeps it near Mach 3 • The flight path: it can fly high, up to about 15 km, and drop to as low as about 5 metres at the end, which makes it harder to detect • The "fire and forget" idea, and the range: about 290 km for the standard version, with newer versions reported at 450 km or more Extra context beyond the video: • Some websites claim BrahMos can carry a nuclear warhead. The official BrahMos site describes a conventional warhead, so we do not make that claim • "World's fastest" depends on how you define the category, so we say "one of the fastest operational cruise missiles" • Range figures vary by version and by report • This video is an educational explainer. We have not added technical details beyond what is publicly available • Based on official BrahMos information and defence reporting, current as of November 24, 2026 Facts, not hype. candidates.title: The Strangest Property of the Electron #physics #quantumphysics
candidates.description: Turn an electron all the way around, one full turn, and it's not back where it started. You have to turn it twice. In under 3 minutes: 1922: Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach fire silver atoms through a specially shaped magnet. Instead of one long stripe, they land in just two spots: up or down 1925: George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit propose the electron spins like a tiny planet, making it a tiny magnet But it can't literally spin: its surface would have to move more than 100 times faster than light, and the electron has no measurable size at all Spin is a built-in twist the electron simply has. Physicists call it angular momentum, always exactly the same amount Turn an electron 360° and its quantum wave flips upside down. Only after 720° is it truly back, tested with neutrons in 1975 Dirac's belt trick shows why two turns can be undone but one can't, built here from the real maths of the trick Spin decides how electrons fill orbitals, gives every element its chemistry, makes iron magnetic and powers MRI scans Episode 21 of a series explaining the universe, one big idea at a time. So, did the belt trick make it click, or is spin still breaking your brain? Tell me in the comments. 👇 Photos: Otto Stern, Walther Gerlach, George Uhlenbeck, Samuel Goudsmit, Paul Dirac. candidates.title: Look closely at the painting of this silk | Carolus-Duran 🔍 #arthistory
candidates.description: Up close, her satin dress is nothing but long, fast strokes of white. Step back and it shines. This is the painting style a young John Singer Sargent learned in Paris. The painting Carolus-Duran signed this portrait in Paris in May 1876 and showed it at the Salon of 1877, where it became known as "the lady with the red cushion". Critics were largely hostile. The red cushion and the colours shocked them, and one said the painter should have held back from "setting off fireworks". The artist Carolus-Duran was one of the most fashionable portrait painters in Paris. He taught his students to paint straight onto the canvas with a loaded brush, wet into wet, with no careful drawing first. In May 1874 an 18-year-old Sargent joined his studio and soon became his star pupil. The sitter Alice de Lancey was born Julia Tahl in Baltimore in 1851 and became a well-known figure in Belle Époque Paris. In 1913 she left the portrait to the Petit Palais, along with Carolus-Duran's portrait of her dog, Chinois. What to look for The face is smooth and finished. The satin is loose and fast. Zoom into the dress and the folds break into single strokes of white and pink. Then watch my Sargent pearls Short (linked under the title) and you'll see where he learned it. 🎨 Mademoiselle de Lancey, Carolus-Duran, 1876, oil on canvas 📍 Petit Palais, Paris I'm Simon Claridge, a British artist. I zoom into great paintings to show you the details you'd walk straight past in a gallery. Follow for more close looks at art history. 🔗 simonclaridge.com #arthistory #CarolusDuran #JohnSingerSargent #Sargent #PetitPalais #oilpainting #brushwork #portraitpainting #belleepoque #lookclosely

GDP is the market value of new goods and services produced in India in one year. Its formula, C+I+G+X-M, also reflects aggregate demand: Consumption, Investment, Government expenditure (for example, buying grain from farmers at Minimum Support Price), plus Exports, minus Imports (not produced in India). After Covid, if the government and RBI cut loan rates and give tax relief, as under the Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative, demand rises quickly but supply cannot catch up at the same speed. GDP appears to grow, but inflation also shoots up. This is overheating. Keynesian economics recommends counter-cyclical fiscal stimulus during a slowdown, but excess stimulus carries this risk. candidates.description: Same load. Two columns. A very different result. 🏗️ Rectangular ties vs spiral reinforcement—what changes inside a reinforced concrete column? The left column bends and cracks in this demonstration, while the spiral-reinforced column on the right remains standing. The key concept is concrete confinement: how transverse reinforcement helps restrain the concrete core and support the vertical reinforcing bars under compression. 🔎 What to look for: • Rectangular ties surrounding the longitudinal rebar. • Continuous spiral reinforcement wrapping around the concrete core. • The developing crack and deformation on the left. • The role of reinforcement detailing in strength and ductility. Ductility is the ability to deform before failure. Properly designed spiral reinforcement can improve confinement and ductility, but column performance depends on much more than its outer shape. 📌 Educational illustration: This is an AI-generated animation, not a physical load test or an engineering calculation. candidates.title: He Only Tested His Invention at Night 🌙 #shorts
candidates.description: He only tested his invention at night, so the neighbours wouldn't think he'd gone mad. Before 1830, a fine lawn meant men with scythes. Edwin Budding, an engineer in the cloth mills near Stroud, England, knew a machine that trimmed the nap off woollen cloth with a spinning bladed cylinder. He adapted the idea for grass: cast-iron rollers, gears and a rotating cylinder of blades. With his partner John Ferrabee he patented the first lawnmower in 1830. Local tradition says the two of them tested it after dark, so nobody would see a grown man pushing a strange machine around a field. Budding's machine was marketed to country gentlemen as healthy exercise, and early ones went to the Zoological Gardens in Regent's Park and to Oxford colleges. Budding is also credited with the adjustable spanner. Would you have mowed in the dark too? Sources: - Wikipedia, "Edwin Beard Budding" and "Lawn mower" - Science Museum Group collection, "Budding's patent lawn mower, 1832" - Country Life, "Curious Questions: Who invented the lawnmower?" Original animation, simplified for a short. The night-testing story is a local tradition rather than a documented fact. #shorts #history #inventions

candidates.title: This 1949 Art Experiment Is Absolutely Fascinating!
candidates.description: What happens when one of the world's greatest artists paints on glass instead of paper? The result is absolutely fascinating! In 1949, legendary Spanish artist Pablo Picasso created an extraordinary art experiment that captured the attention of viewers. Instead of painting on a traditional canvas, Picasso drew directly onto a sheet of glass while a camera filmed from the opposite side. As his hand moved across the glass, bold and flowing lines gradually transformed into the shape of a beautiful bird. The camera revealed every artistic movement, allowing viewers to watch the entire creation process from a unique perspective. This fascinating technique showed how creativity can turn an ordinary surface into something extraordinary. Picasso's ability to create recognizable shapes using just a few confident lines demonstrates why his artistic imagination continues to inspire people around the world. This short video explores a remarkable moment in art history, showcasing Picasso's experimental approach to drawing and his incredible creative vision. candidates.title: Sum vs Integration Explained Visually | Riemann Sum, Area Under Curve & Calculus #integration #area
candidates.description: Explore the beautiful connection between summation and integration through a clear and visually engaging mathematical demonstration. This video explains how a Riemann Sum gradually approaches a definite integral as the number of rectangles increases, making one of the most important concepts in calculus easier to understand. The visualization focuses on the function y = x⁴ and demonstrates how the area beneath a curve can be approximated using rectangular sections. Each rectangle represents a small contribution to the total area. As the number of rectangles increases, their widths become smaller and the approximation becomes more accurate, approaching the exact value of the definite integral. The video presents the relationship between discrete summation and continuous integration in an intuitive way. It highlights the fundamental idea behind integral calculus, numerical approximation, area estimation, and the transition from finite sums to the limit of infinitely many subdivisions. The Riemann Sum is an essential concept in calculus because it provides a foundation for understanding definite integrals. By dividing an interval into smaller sections, evaluating the function at selected points, and adding the resulting rectangular areas, we can approximate the total area under a curve. Integration extends this idea by taking the limit as the width of the subdivisions approaches zero. This mathematical visualization also demonstrates the importance of increasing the number of rectangles. With fewer rectangles, the approximation may differ noticeably from the exact integral. With more rectangles, the approximation becomes increasingly refined, illustrating the mathematical principle that connects summation with integration. This topic is useful for students learning calculus, mathematics enthusiasts exploring mathematical concepts, teachers explaining graphical interpretations of integration, and learners preparing for advanced mathematics examinations. It supports conceptual understanding of definite integrals, Riemann sums, limits, functions, graphical analysis, and numerical integration. The channel explores calculus, algebra, geometry, mathematical functions, equations, formulas, and other fascinating areas of mathematics through visually rich educational content. This video is suitable for mathematics students, calculus beginners, competitive examination learners, educators, and anyone interested in understanding the connection between mathematical formulas and their graphical meaning. candidates.title: Boom and Bust: The 3 Forces That Run the Economy
candidates.description: Boom and bust explained: three forces run the economy. Productivity makes us richer slowly, while two debt cycles make it feel like a roller coaster. In 1800, light cost about nine thousand times more work than it did by 1990, according to economist William Nordhaus. Candles gave way to oil lamps, gas lamps and the light bulb, each squeezing more light out of an hour of work. That is productivity: slow, steady, and the reason living standards rise over centuries. On top of it sit two louder forces: a short-term debt cycle of about five to eight years (booms and recessions) and a long-term debt cycle of about 75 to 100 years (like the 1930s and 2008). Up close it looks like chaos; step back and the escalator still goes up. Part 6 of "How the Economy Really Works". Idea inspired by Ray Dalio's "How The Economic Machine Works". The story, script and animation are our own. Sources: - William D. Nordhaus, "Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not", in The Economics of New Goods (NBER, 1996): https://www.nber.org/books-and-chapters/economics-new-goods/do-real-output-and-real-wage-measures-capture-reality-history-lighting-suggests-not - Ray Dalio, "How The Economic Machine Works" (2013), for the three forces and the cycle lengths Voice: Kokoro TTS (Apache 2.0). 3D trees: Kenney (CC0). candidates.title: Why Is This Country Stuck Inside Senegal? 🌍 #geography #facts #shorts
candidates.description: Gambia is a sliver of land surrounded by Senegal, defined entirely by the path of the Gambia River. This geography is the result of 19th-century colonial rivalry, where British and French interests fought for control over the river and the surrounding territory. Understanding the Gambia River explains why the nation exists as an enclave today. The border follows the riverbanks, leaving the country isolated within its larger neighbor. This unique political geography demonstrates how historical claims by European empires permanently altered the map of Africa. candidates.title: Why can't your hands pass through each other? (Answer: Quantum mechanics)
candidates.description: Why can't my hands go through each other? Atoms are almost entirely empty space, so what's pushing back? The answer comes down to a strange fact about electrons: turn one by a full turn and it doesn't come back. You have to turn it twice! candidates.title: Why does a V8 sound like THAT? 🔊#engineering #gaming #physics #pixelart #engineeringexplained #retro
candidates.description: Play this V8 + get its full soundtrack → link in bio 🎮🎧 A V8 fires a bang every quarter turn, perfectly evenly. But its crank is a cross, so each side's exhaust gets its 4 bangs unevenly. Two pipes, two lopsided rhythms: that IS the rumble. (A flat-plane crank alternates the sides evenly, and the rumble's gone.) 🎮 V8 LAB: swap the firing order, flip the crank, hear the beat change, rev it till it breaks 🎧 THE FULL V8 SOUNDTRACK: this beat, 2 minutes long 👉 Both at the link in bio · 8bitengineering.org 📚 SOURCES • Firing order 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2 + the 350's 101.6 × 88.4 mm bore and stroke: Wikipedia, "Chevrolet small-block engine (1954–2003)" • Cross-plane crank, even firing overall but uneven on each bank: Wikipedia, "Crossplane" • Uneven pulses on each bank = the V8 rumble: Toyota Times, "Behind the Engine Tones that are Music to the Ears of Car Lovers" · Car Throttle, "Why Do Different Engine Configurations Make Different Sounds?" · BBC Science Focus, "Why do V8 engines sound so good?" • Braps = unburnt fuel going off in the hot exhaust: Wikipedia, "Back-fire" • 55 bangs a second at idle: 825 rpm ÷ 60 × 4 = 55 ⚠️ HEADS UP No real engine recordings in this video. Every engine sound is synthesized from the animation's own crank, so sound and picture stay locked together, even in slow-mo. Real V8 recordings were only a tone reference; none of their audio is in here. The slow-mo bangs are designed sounds, and the beat is original. The engine is a simplified illustration (a generic cross-plane V8 with the small-block Chevy's firing order), and the revs and pops are timed to the beat. Not affiliated with any car maker. #v8 #engine #howitworks #pixelart #carsound

candidates.title: Episode 06: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors (Vectors That Refuse to Turn) #shorts #ai #math #byteai
candidates.description: Forget memorizing det(A - λI) = 0! What is an eigenvector in real life? 🧭⚡ When a matrix transforms space, almost EVERY vector gets rotated and knocked off its original span line. Except for very special directions: EIGENVECTORS! 🎯 1️⃣ While the rest of space spins or shears, an eigenvector stays LOCKED on its exact same span line. It refuses to turn! 2️⃣ The only thing that happens to it is stretching or shrinking. 3️⃣ The scale factor of that stretch? That is the EIGENVALUE (λ)! If λ = 2.0, the vector simply doubles in length without changing its direction. 🧠 Why Machine Learning & AI Care: In Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and modern AI, eigenvectors reveal the exact axes of maximum variance in giant datasets. Instead of 1,000 messy features, we compress the data along its most informative eigenvector axes! 🚀 Next up in Episode 07: The Dot Product (Similarity in Vector Space)! 🔔 Follow @byteai3.14 for visual, intuitive AI math! #eigenvalues #eigenvectors #linearalgebra #pca #datascience #machinelearning #artificialintelligence #deeplearning #mathematics #stem #tech #byteai #manim #animation

candidates.description: महाराष्ट्र के बुलढाणा जिले में स्थित लोनार झील एक प्राचीन उल्कापिंड की टक्कर से बना दुनिया का एक अद्भुत प्राकृतिक और रहस्यमयी स्थल है। लोनार झील के मुख्य रहस्य और तथ्य • उल्कापिंड से निर्माण: वैज्ञानिकों के अनुसार, लगभग 50,000 से 570,000 साल पहले अंतरिक्ष से एक तेज रफ्तार उल्कापिंड या धूमकेतु यहाँ पृथ्वी से टकराया था। इस भयंकर टक्कर से करीब 1.8 किलोमीटर व्यास और 150 मीटर गहरा विशाल गड्ढा बना, जो बाद में झील में बदल गया। • बेसाल्ट चट्टानों में इकलौती झील: यह पृथ्वी पर बेसाल्ट चट्टानों (ज्वालामुखीय लावा से बनी काली चट्टानों) के बीच बने दुनिया के चुनिंदा क्रेटरों में से एक है। नासा और दुनिया भर के वैज्ञानिकों के अनुसार, इसकी बनावट काफी हद तक मंगल ग्रह की सतह से मिलती-जुलती है। • खारा और क्षारीय पानी: इस झील का पानी सामान्य झीलों की तरह मीठा नहीं है, बल्कि यह अत्यधिक खारा (Saline) और क्षारीय (Alkaline) है। इसमें नमक और कई खास खनिजों की मात्रा बहुत अधिक है। • अचानक गुलाबी रंग बदलना: जून 2020 में लोनार झील का पानी रातों-रात हरे से गुलाबी (या लाल) रंग का हो गया था। वैज्ञानिकों की रिसर्च के अनुसार, पानी में मौजूद खास तरह के हेलोआर्किया (Haloarchaea) सूक्ष्मजीवों, शैवाल (Algae) और बढ़ते खारेपन के कारण इसका रंग बदलता है। • प्राचीन मंदिर और इतिहास: इस झील के चारों ओर लगभग 1,000 साल पुराने कई प्राचीन मंदिर हैं, जिनमें भगवान विष्णु, सूर्य, और दुर्गा को समर्पित दैत्यासुदन मंदिर प्रमुख है, जिसकी नक्काशी खजुराहो के मंदिरों से मिलती-जुलती है। पद्म पुराण और स्कंद पुराण जैसे प्राचीन ग्रंथों में भी इस झील का उल्लेख मिलता है। #short #indian #geography #astronomy #architecture #jheel #jaymaharashtra #indiangeography

candidates.title: Why a Coffee Cup and a Donut Are the Same Shape (Topology Explained)
candidates.description: To a mathematician, a coffee cup and a donut are the same shape. ☕🍩 This is topology, the study of properties that stay the same when you stretch, bend, or squeeze an object without tearing or gluing. A mug has one handle-like hole going all the way through it, and so does a donut. Squish the cup’s bowl down, grow the handle, and you get a donut, with no cutting required. Mathematicians say the two are homeomorphic, and both have genus 1. A sphere is different. It has no through-hole, so you can’t turn it into a donut without tearing a hole in it. 🔴 Topology ignores size, thickness, and curvature and focuses on the underlying structure that links seemingly different shapes. In this short, you’ll learn: ✅ What topology studies ✅ What a through-hole and genus are ✅ What homeomorphic means ✅ Why a sphere can’t become a donut without tearing 👍 Like if this changed how you see your coffee cup 💬 Comment: What everyday object would you try next, a pretzel, a pair of glasses, or a bowl? 🔔 Subscribe for more math, physics, and chemistry explained clearly ↗️ Share with someone who loves puzzles or math #Shorts #Topology #Math #Mathematics #Donut #CoffeeCup #Geometry #STEM #MathExplained #ScienceExplained
